g.text: Prompt caching and cost: what one call costs in tokens, time and money, what a stable
prefix saves, and what silently breaks a cache.
lessons/16-prompt-caching-and-cost/run.py (the prompts live here; the exercises ask
The story below is the setting. LANTERN is the local model; the case files are the text you send it.
A request from headquarters, two lines long. Every force in the region wants LANTERN's message
classifier: about forty thousand intercepted messages a month between them. What would a year cost, and
would a hosted model, used only on synthetic training material, be cheaper or faster?
Varma passes it to you. "Not a guess," she says. "Measure what one call costs us here, then work out
what it would cost there. And tell me what makes the difference."
sorting-guide.md (first lines; the whole guide is the fixed part of every call)
Prepared by D. Okafor, Economic Offences Wing, for LANTERN's message classifier. Version 3.
Every example below is invented for training. None is taken from an exhibit.
Every message gets exactly one label.
Locally a call costs nothing in money: it costs time, and the time is mostly the prompt.
Ollama's `prompt_eval_count` counts only the tokens it had to process: the same prefix again reported
messages, the guide always in front
. Something that changes, first: the same
The same 48 messages, two layouts (qwen3:1.7b, temperature 0)
Same guide, same messages, same answers: only the order of the bytes changed.
Two consecutive requests: where do they stop matching?
two tools, order swapped each call
hits here: qwen3's chat template puts the tool list after the system
text, so the guide in front stayed cached and only what followed it changed. Anthropic renders tools before
the system prompt, so the same swap there invalidates the whole prefix. Sort tools by name and build them
once, and the order never matters.
Other silent breakers: a date in the system prompt, a dict serialised in a different order, a per-user line
near the top, a changed model or a different thinking setting.
. A year of messages on a hosted model: an estimate, not a measurement
Estimate for claude-haiku-5-5: prices from config.yaml (checked 2026-11-21), token
counts from this run's Qwen tokenizer
per correct answer, at this run's 71%
day's messages into one huge prompt can cost more, not less.
Every number in this table is price arithmetic on token counts, not a hosted run. The hosted run is `make
`, which reads cached tokens from the reply.
1. In step 1, compare the prompt tokens of the fresh prefix with the same prefix again. What does
Ollama's count leave out, and what would a hosted bill count?
2. In step 3, the two layouts sent the same guide. Why did only one of them reuse it?
3. In step 5, which line of the estimate would change if the model's tokenizer were different, and
1. In run.py, in stable(), add f"Today is {datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}." to the start of the
system content. How many cache hits are left?
2. In run.py, in varying(), move the header from the start of the system content to the start of the
user turn. Do the hits come back?
3. In run.py, cut the worked examples out of the guide you send (GUIDE.split('## Worked
examples')[0]). What happens to the year estimate, and to the correct count?
4. No edit: run LANTERN_MODEL=qwen3:4b make lesson N=16. Does the speedup grow or shrink with a larger
More detail: 'Try this' in lessons/16-prompt-caching-and-cost/README.md. Undo an edit with git checkout
<file>, or set every change aside with git stash.
On LANTERN a call costs nothing but time, and most of the time is the prompt. With the sorting guide
first and the message last, 48 of 48 calls reused the cached guide and prompt processing was 20.3 times
faster. A request ID in the first line cut the reuse to 0, with the same guide and the same answers.
The hosted cost is price arithmetic until a hosted run measures it, and the screen says so.
Varma reads the line that says it is an estimate twice. "Then the next thing we prove," she says, "is
that LANTERN can take forty thousand messages without falling over."
